# Load Balancing

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A **load balancer's** only job is deciding, for every incoming request, which of several identical backend servers should handle it, so no single server ever becomes the bottleneck.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### A load balancer in front of a fleet of servers

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    s1["Server A"]:::server
    s2["Server B"]:::server
    s3["Server C (unhealthy)"]:::server
    client --> lb
    lb -->|"routed"| s1
    lb -->|"routed"| s2
    lb -.->|"health check fails"| s3
```

#### Round robin vs least connections

| Round robin | Least connections |
| :--- | :--- |
| Cycles through servers in fixed order, ignoring current load | Sends each request to the server with the fewest active connections |
| Simple, cheap, works well when requests and servers are uniform | Adapts to uneven request cost or server capacity automatically |
| Can overload a server that's already slow, since it doesn't know | Needs the load balancer to track live connection counts per server |

#### Health check state transitions

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  healthy["Healthy: in rotation"]
  checking["Health check fails"]
  unhealthy["Unhealthy: removed"]
  recheck["Health check passes"]
  healthy --> checking
  checking --> unhealthy
  unhealthy --> recheck
  recheck --> healthy
```

#### Response latency vs load on a single server

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Assuming a load balancer is a single simple box==, when production systems almost always run it in pairs with a failover mechanism.
- ⚠️ Using sticky sessions to work around server-local state, then being surprised when one heavy client makes one server hot while others sit idle.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that health checks need tuning: ==too aggressive and a temporarily slow-but-fine server gets pulled unnecessarily==; too lax and a dead server keeps receiving traffic for too long.
- ⚠️ Treating load balancing as purely a server-layer concern and forgetting that a global (DNS/geo) layer usually sits above the local one in any system with more than one data center.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: When would you choose least connections over round robin?**

> **Model Answer:** When requests vary significantly in how expensive they are to handle, or when your servers aren't uniform in capacity. Round robin assumes every request and server is roughly equal; **least connections** adapts to real-time load, so a server stuck processing a few slow requests naturally receives fewer new ones.

**Q: Why is a lone load balancer considered a design flaw even if it's fast and correctly configured?**

> **Model Answer:** It's a ==single point of failure==: if that one instance goes down, every server behind it becomes unreachable even though they're all healthy. Production systems run at least two load balancers with a failover mechanism (like a floating IP or DNS-based redundancy) so the load-balancing layer itself survives one instance dying.

# Distributed Caching Deep Dive

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A **cache** is a bet that the same data will be asked for again soon, and every hard caching problem, stampedes, hot keys, eviction, is really just a case where that bet briefly stops paying off.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Cache-aside pattern with a stampede in progress

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    app["App Server"]:::server
    cache["Distributed Cache"]:::cache
    db[("Database")]:::db
    client --> app
    app -->|"read, key just expired"| cache
    app -.->|"cache miss, many requests at once"| db
    app -.->|"write result back"| cache
```

#### Redis vs Memcached

| Redis | Memcached |
| :--- | :--- |
| Rich data structures: lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes | Pure key-value byte-string cache, nothing else |
| Optional persistence to disk and built-in replication | No persistence, purely in-memory, simpler internals |
| Also usable as a lightweight message broker (pub/sub) or database | Multithreaded by default, often faster for plain get/set at scale |

#### Cache hit rate vs cache size (diminishing returns)

#### Choosing a stampede prevention technique

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  expire["Hot key about to expire"] --> choice{"Which defense fits?"}
  choice -->|"simplest"| lock["Lock: one request recomputes, rest wait"]
  choice -->|"spread the risk"| jitter["Add TTL jitter across keys"]
  choice -->|"best user experience"| swr["Serve stale, refresh in background"]
  lock --> safe["Database sees at most one refresh"]
  jitter --> safe
  swr --> safe
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Setting every cache entry's TTL to the exact same value, which ==guarantees mass expiration== and turns a routine refresh into a stampede.
- ⚠️ Assuming a distributed cache automatically balances load evenly, when a single very popular key can still saturate one node regardless of how well the rest of the keys are spread.
- ⚠️ Treating LRU as a free, always-correct default without considering that a short traffic burst can evict genuinely important, steadily-used data.
- ⚠️ Using the cache as if it were guaranteed durable storage, then ==losing data on a restart== because Memcached, or Redis without persistence enabled, was never meant to be a source of truth.
- ⚠️ Reaching for a distributed cache to fix a hot key problem, when the actual fix is usually a smaller, local in-process cache layered on top of it.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: How would you prevent a cache stampede on a very popular key that refreshes every 60 seconds?**

> **Model Answer:** Use a lock so only one request recomputes the value while the rest wait for it or briefly serve the old value (stale-while-revalidate), or add jitter so the TTL isn't identical for every request that cached the value, or use probabilistic early expiration so refreshes get spread out before the hard expiry instead of all landing on it.

**Q: Your metrics show one Redis node at 100% CPU while the rest of the cluster is nearly idle. What's happening and how do you fix it?**

> **Model Answer:** This is almost certainly a hot key: one key's traffic is concentrated on the single node responsible for it under consistent hashing, which can't split one key's load across nodes. Fixes include adding a small local in-process cache for the hottest keys on each app server, or splitting the hot key into several suffixed copies and picking one at random on read.

**Q: When would you choose LFU over LRU for eviction?**

> **Model Answer:** When you have data that's consistently, heavily accessed but could be temporarily overshadowed by a short burst of unrelated one-time traffic, like a product catalog's best-sellers versus a flash-sale item. LFU protects the steadily popular items from eviction in that scenario, where LRU would incorrectly treat the recent burst as more relevant.

lesson.content:
# Consistent Hashing

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> **Consistent hashing** exists so that adding or removing one server only reshuffles a small slice of your data, instead of almost all of it.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Consistent hashing ring with a server added

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    k1["Key: user_42"]:::client
    k2["Key: user_88"]:::client
    s1["Server A"]:::server
    s2["Server B"]:::server
    s3["Server C (new)"]:::server
    k1 -->|"unchanged"| s1
    k2 -->|"moved from B to C"| s3
```

#### Modulo hashing vs consistent hashing

| hash(key) % N | Consistent hashing |
| :--- | :--- |
| Simple to implement and understand | Keys and servers share one fixed ring, independent of N |
| Changing N remaps nearly every key | Adding or removing a server only moves that server's share of keys |
| A single server change causes a mass data-movement event | Needs virtual nodes to keep load evenly distributed |

#### Keys remapped when adding one server

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Implementing consistent hashing with only one ring position per server and being surprised when load is wildly uneven, that unevenness is exactly what virtual nodes exist to fix.
- ⚠️ Confusing consistent hashing with plain hashing, they solve different problems, plain hashing distributes evenly for a fixed N, consistent hashing minimizes movement when N changes.
- ⚠️ ==Assuming consistent hashing guarantees perfectly equal load at all times==, it guarantees minimal movement on change, even distribution is a secondary benefit that depends on enough virtual nodes.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that adding a server still means that server starts cold, with none of the data now mapped to it actually cached or replicated there yet, a warm-up period is still needed.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why doesn't `hash(key) % N` work well for a cache cluster that scales up and down?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the modulo operation depends on the exact current value of N, changing N even by one server changes the result for almost every key, causing a mass simultaneous cache miss or data migration exactly when the system is already changing capacity.

**Q: What problem do virtual nodes solve in consistent hashing, and why can't you just add more physical servers instead?**

> **Model Answer:** With only one ring position per physical server, load distribution depends on the luck of where each server's single hash landed, which can be very uneven. Virtual nodes give each physical server many scattered ring positions, so its total share of keys becomes an average of many small slices instead of one arc, evening out load without needing any more actual servers.

# Database Indexing & Query Performance

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> An **index** is a separate, sorted structure built purely to make reads fast, and every index you add makes writes a little slower and storage a little bigger, so indexing is always a trade, not a free upgrade.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Query path with and without an index

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    app["App Server"]:::server
    idx["Index (B-tree)"]:::cache
    table[("Table (full data)")]:::db
    app -->|"lookup by indexed column"| idx
    idx -->|"jump to matching rows"| table
    app -.->|"full scan if no usable index"| table
```

#### With an index vs without

| With an index | Without an index |
| :--- | :--- |
| Reads jump close to the matching rows, roughly logarithmic time | Reads scan every row, linear time in table size |
| Every insert, update, delete also updates the index structure | Writes only touch the table, nothing extra to maintain |
| Extra disk space for the index itself | No extra storage beyond the table |

#### Rows examined: indexed lookup vs full table scan

#### Will the query planner actually use this index?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  q["Query arrives"] --> covered{"Does an index cover the leftmost filter columns?"}
  covered -->|"no"| scan["Full table scan"]
  covered -->|"yes"| big{"Would it return most of the table anyway?"}
  big -->|"yes"| scan
  big -->|"no"| fn{"Is a function applied to the column?"}
  fn -->|"yes"| scan
  fn -->|"no"| use["Planner uses the index"]
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Adding an index for every column that ever appears in a WHERE clause, without noticing the ==cumulative write cost== across many indexes on the same table.
- ⚠️ Building a composite index in the wrong column order, then being confused why a query filtering on the second column alone gets a full scan.
- ⚠️ Assuming an index exists means it's being used, without ever checking an actual query plan (EXPLAIN) to confirm it.
- ⚠️ Wrapping an indexed column in a function in the query (like `WHERE LOWER(email) = ...`) and not realizing that ==prevents the plain index== on `email` from being used at all.
- ⚠️ Indexing a low-cardinality boolean or status column expecting a big speedup, when the index barely narrows the result set down.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why doesn't adding an index always speed up a query?**

> **Model Answer:** The query planner only uses an index when it estimates that doing so is cheaper than a full scan, which isn't true when the query returns a large fraction of the table, when a function or type conversion is applied to the indexed column, or when the column's data statistics are stale. Indexes also don't help if the query filters on columns not covered by the leftmost prefix of a composite index.

**Q: You have a composite index on (user_id, created_at). Will a query that filters only on created_at use it efficiently?**

> **Model Answer:** Generally no. Composite indexes are sorted by their leftmost column first, so an index on (user_id, created_at) is effectively useless for a query that filters on created_at alone without also constraining user_id, because the created_at values aren't contiguous in the index without knowing user_id first.

**Q: What's the real cost of adding an index to a write-heavy table?**

> **Model Answer:** Every insert, update, or delete that touches the indexed column has to also update the index's B-tree structure, which adds latency to every write and adds disk space for the index itself. On a table with many indexes, a single insert can mean updating several separate B-trees, which compounds quickly on high-write OLTP tables.

    idx["Index (B-tree)"]:::cache

    idx -->|"jump to matching rows"| table

```

#### With an index vs without

| With an index | Without an index |
| :--- | :--- |
| Reads jump close to the matching rows, roughly logarithmic time | Reads scan every row, linear time in table size |
| Every insert, update, delete also updates the index structure | Writes only touch the table, nothing extra to maintain |
| Extra disk space for the index itself | No extra storage beyond the table |

#### Rows examined: indexed lookup vs full table scan

#### Will the query planner actually use this index?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  q["Query arrives"] --> covered{"Does an index cover the leftmost filter columns?"}
  covered -->|"no"| scan["Full table scan"]
  covered -->|"yes"| big{"Would it return most of the table anyway?"}
  big -->|"yes"| scan
  big -->|"no"| fn{"Is a function applied to the column?"}
  fn -->|"yes"| scan
  fn -->|"no"| use["Planner uses the index"]
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Adding an index for every column that ever appears in a WHERE clause, without noticing the ==cumulative write cost== across many indexes on the same table.
- ⚠️ Building a composite index in the wrong column order, then being confused why a query filtering on the second column alone gets a full scan.
- ⚠️ Assuming an index exists means it's being used, without ever checking an actual query plan (EXPLAIN) to confirm it.
- ⚠️ Wrapping an indexed column in a function in the query (like `WHERE LOWER(email) = ...`) and not realizing that ==prevents the plain index== on `email` from being used at all.
- ⚠️ Indexing a low-cardinality boolean or status column expecting a big speedup, when the index barely narrows the result set down.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why doesn't adding an index always speed up a query?**

> **Model Answer:** The query planner only uses an index when it estimates that doing so is cheaper than a full scan, which isn't true when the query returns a large fraction of the table, when a function or type conversion is applied to the indexed column, or when the column's data statistics are stale. **Q: You have a composite index on (user_id, created_at). Will a query that filters only on created_at use it efficiently?**

> **Model Answer:** Generally no. Composite indexes are sorted by their leftmost column first, so an index on (user_id, created_at) is effectively useless for a query that filters on created_at alone without also constraining user_id, because the created_at values aren't contiguous in the index without knowing user_id first.

**Q: What's the real cost of adding an index to a write-heavy table?**

> **Model Answer:** Every insert, update, or delete that touches the indexed column has to also update the index's B-tree structure, which adds latency to every write and adds disk space for the index itself. On a table with many indexes, a single insert can mean updating several separate B-trees, which compounds quickly on high-write OLTP tables.

# Message Queues & Stream Processing

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A log-based system like **Kafka** doesn't hand a message to one consumer and forget it, it keeps an ordered, replayable record that many independent consumers can each read at their own pace.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Topic with partitions and two independent consumer groups

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    producer["Producer"]:::server
    p0>"Partition 0"]:::queue
    p1>"Partition 1"]:::queue
    cg1["Consumer Group A"]:::server
    cg2["Consumer Group B"]:::server
    producer -->|"keyed by user_id"| p0
    producer -->|"keyed by user_id"| p1
    p0 -->|"reads independently"| cg1
    p1 -->|"reads independently"| cg1
    p0 -.->|"same events, separate offset"| cg2
    p1 -.->|"same events, separate offset"| cg2
```

#### Traditional queue vs log-based streaming

| Traditional queue (classic) | Log-based streaming (Kafka-style) |
| :--- | :--- |
| A message is removed once a consumer reads it | Messages persist for a retention window, reading doesn't delete |
| Great for handing out discrete jobs to exactly one worker | Many independent consumer groups can read the same stream separately |
| No built-in replay of past messages | Supports replay by resetting a consumer group's offset |

#### Offset commit timing and crash risk

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant P as Partition
  participant C as Consumer
  P->>C: deliver message
  Note over C: commit offset early
  C->>C: crash mid-processing
  Note over C: message lost on restart
  P->>C: deliver message
  C->>C: process fully first
  C->>P: commit offset late
  Note over C: safe, but retry may duplicate
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Assuming a topic guarantees global ordering== across all its events, when the guarantee only holds within a single partition.
- ⚠️ Choosing a poor partition key (like a constant, or something with very few distinct values) that funnels almost all traffic onto one partition and defeats the whole point of partitioning.
- ⚠️ Treating Kafka like a traditional task queue and being surprised messages aren't deleted after being read, or that retention, not consumption, controls when data disappears.
- ⚠️ ==Committing offsets before processing finishes==, then losing messages on a crash, or committing well after processing without idempotency, causing duplicate processing on retry.
- ⚠️ Adding consumers to a group expecting more parallelism than the topic actually has partitions, a group can never usefully have more active consumers than partitions.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only within a partition, not across a whole topic?**

> **Model Answer:** Ordering across the entire topic would require a single, global sequence, which kills parallelism, only one writer or reader could safely proceed at a time. By guaranteeing order only within a partition (typically by hashing a key so related events land together), Kafka lets many partitions be written and read in parallel while still preserving the ordering that actually matters, like all of one user's events staying in sequence.

**Q: Two different services need to react to the same 'order_placed' event, but with completely different processing logic. How does a log-based system make that easy?**

> **Model Answer:** Each service runs its own consumer group reading the same topic, and consumer groups track their own offsets independently. Neither group's read position affects the other, and since reading doesn't delete the message, both can process the full stream of events at their own pace without any coordination between them.

**Q: What's the risk of committing a consumer's offset immediately after receiving a message, before processing finishes?**

> **Model Answer:** If the consumer crashes while processing, the offset has already advanced past that message, so on restart the consumer resumes after it and the message is ==silently never processed==, effectively lost. The safer pattern is to commit the offset only after processing succeeds, accepting that a crash mid-processing might cause the message to be reprocessed, which is why consumers should be built to handle **duplicate delivery**.

lesson.content:
# Distributed Unique ID Generation

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Once more than one machine can create new rows at the same time, a single **auto-incrementing counter** stops being possible, so distributed systems need an ID scheme that many machines can generate correctly without ever talking to each other.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Snowflake-style ID generation across shards

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    w1["Worker 1 (server A)"]:::server
    w2["Worker 2 (server B)"]:::server
    coord["Worker ID assignment"]:::server
    db[("Sharded Database")]:::db
    coord -->|"assigns worker_id=1"| w1
    coord -->|"assigns worker_id=2"| w2
    w1 -->|"generates ID locally, no round trip"| db
    w2 -->|"generates ID locally, no round trip"| db
```

#### UUID v4 vs Snowflake-style ID

| UUID v4 | Snowflake-style ID |
| :--- | :--- |
| 128 bits, fully random, effectively zero collision risk | 64 bits, packs timestamp + worker ID + sequence |
| No inherent time ordering, sorts randomly | Roughly sortable by creation time |
| Zero coordination needed, not even a worker ID to assign | Needs a scheme to assign unique worker IDs to each generator |

#### Two workers generating IDs, same millisecond, no coordination

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant W1 as Worker 1
  participant W2 as Worker 2
  W1->>W1: timestamp + worker_id=1 + seq=0
  W2->>W2: timestamp + worker_id=2 + seq=0
  W1->>W1: ID = ...worker_id 1
  W2->>W2: ID = ...worker_id 2
  Note over W1,W2: Same millisecond, no collision
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Trying to keep auto-increment IDs after sharding by having each shard start at a different offset, which works briefly but breaks the moment you add another shard or run out of the allocated range.
- ⚠️ Using UUID v4 as a primary key on a huge, high-write table without realizing the random insert order fragments the index and hurts write throughput compared to a roughly sequential key.
- ⚠️ ==Assuming Snowflake-style IDs are perfectly globally ordered==, they're only roughly ordered, clock skew between machines and network delay mean two IDs close in time aren't a guaranteed strict ordering.
- ⚠️ Forgetting to plan worker ID assignment before deploying a Snowflake-style generator, then having two machines accidentally reuse the same worker ID and start colliding.
- ⚠️ Exposing an auto-increment-style ID publicly (like in a URL) and inadvertently leaking how many total records exist or letting users guess adjacent IDs, a problem neither UUIDs nor Snowflake-style IDs have to the same degree.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't you just keep using auto-increment IDs once you shard your database across multiple machines?**

> **Model Answer:** Auto-increment relies on a single counter that every insert goes through, which is exactly what sharding removes, each shard would generate its own sequence independently and eventually produce duplicate IDs across shards, making merges, joins, and global uniqueness impossible to guarantee.

**Q: What does a Snowflake-style ID offer that a UUID doesn't, and what does it cost to get that?**

> **Model Answer:** A Snowflake-style ID is roughly sortable by creation time and fits in a compact 64-bit integer, both useful for pagination, debugging, and index locality, which a random UUID can't offer. The cost is that you need a scheme to assign each ID-generating machine a unique worker ID, some coordination UUIDs don't require at all.

**Q: Why can inserting UUID v4 primary keys into a B-tree index hurt write performance at scale, compared to a roughly sequential ID?**

> **Model Answer:** B-tree indexes perform best when new keys land near the existing high end of the tree, which sequential or roughly time-ordered IDs naturally do. Fully random UUIDs scatter inserts across the entire key space, causing far more page splits and index fragmentation, which shows up as slower writes and a larger, less cache-friendly index over time.

lesson.content:
# Distributed Consensus Basics

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> **Consensus** is how a group of machines that don't fully trust each other's timing or health still agree on one true answer, and the whole difficulty comes from never being able to tell the difference between 'that node is slow' and 'that node is dead'.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Quorum write across five replicas

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    leader["Leader"]:::server
    n1[("Replica 1")]:::db
    n2[("Replica 2")]:::db
    n3[("Replica 3")]:::db
    n4[("Replica 4 (unreachable)")]:::db
    client -->|"write request"| leader
    leader -->|"ack"| n1
    leader -->|"ack"| n2
    leader -->|"ack"| n3
    leader -.->|"no response, quorum already reached"| n4
```

#### Paxos vs Raft

| Paxos | Raft |
| :--- | :--- |
| Prepare then accept phases, proven correct, foundational | Explicit leader election as a first-class, separate phase |
| Deliberately general, doesn't prescribe a single leader model | Log replication and safety rules kept clearly distinct |
| Notoriously hard to reason about and implement correctly | Designed from the start to be understandable and implementable |

#### Raft-style leader failover

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant L as Leader (term 1)
  participant A as Node A
  participant B as Node B
  L->>A: heartbeat
  L->>B: heartbeat
  Note over L: Leader crashes
  A->>B: request vote (term 2)
  B-->>A: vote granted
  Note over A: Majority reached, A becomes leader
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Assuming a quorum of any size works, when W + R > N is specifically what guarantees read and write quorums overlap, ==get that math wrong== and you can read stale data with full confidence it's current.
- ⚠️ Treating an unreachable node as definitely dead, when the entire point of consensus design is that you can never actually know that, only that a majority proceeded without it.
- ⚠️ Building a system with two nodes each able to independently accept writes without a real leader election mechanism, which is exactly how split-brain happens.
- ⚠️ Assuming Paxos or Raft guarantees ==zero downtime==, they guarantee the group never agrees on conflicting values, but a period with no elected leader is genuinely unavailable for writes until election completes.
- ⚠️ Confusing consensus (agreeing on one value or order of operations) with simple replication (copying data to multiple places), replication without a consensus mechanism can still end up with conflicting versions of the truth.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does requiring a majority for both reads and writes guarantee a read always sees the latest write?**

> **Model Answer:** Any two majorities out of N nodes are mathematically guaranteed to share at least one common node, because two disjoint majorities would together need more than N nodes to exist. That shared node participated in the latest successful write, so it's guaranteed to be included in any subsequent read quorum, meaning the read is guaranteed to see the latest value somewhere among the nodes it queries.

**Q: What problem does leader election actually solve in a consensus protocol like Raft?**

> **Model Answer:** Without a leader, every node would need to negotiate the order of every operation with every other node, which is slow and complex. Electing one leader for a period of time lets that leader unilaterally decide the order of operations and replicate them to followers, dramatically simplifying agreement, while the protocol still safely detects a failed leader and elects a new one with a higher term to take over.

**Q: Why is it wrong to say Paxos or Raft guarantees a system will never be unavailable?**

> **Model Answer:** These protocols guarantee safety, the group will never agree on two conflicting values, not liveness in every situation. If a leader fails, there is a real window where no writes can be accepted until a new leader is elected, and in some network partition scenarios a minority side of the cluster can't make progress at all, by design, since it can't reach quorum.

```

#### Paxos vs Raft

| Paxos | Raft |
| :--- | :--- |
| Prepare then accept phases, proven correct, foundational | Explicit leader election as a first-class, separate phase |
| Deliberately general, doesn't prescribe a single leader model | Log replication and safety rules kept clearly distinct |
| Notoriously hard to reason about and implement correctly | Designed from the start to be understandable and implementable |

#### Raft-style leader failover

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant L as Leader (term 1)
  participant A as Node A
  participant B as Node B
  L->>A: heartbeat
  L->>B: heartbeat
  Note over L: Leader crashes
  A->>B: request vote (term 2)
  B-->>A: vote granted
  Note over A: Majority reached, A becomes leader
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Assuming a quorum of any size works, when W + R > N is specifically what guarantees read and write quorums overlap, ==get that math wrong== and you can read stale data with full confidence it's current.
- ⚠️ Treating an unreachable node as definitely dead, when the entire point of consensus design is that you can never actually know that, only that a majority proceeded without it.
- ⚠️ Building a system with two nodes each able to independently accept writes without a real leader election mechanism, which is exactly how split-brain happens.
- ⚠️ Assuming Paxos or Raft guarantees ==zero downtime==, they guarantee the group never agrees on conflicting values, but a period with no elected leader is genuinely unavailable for writes until election completes.
- ⚠️ Confusing consensus (agreeing on one value or order of operations) with simple replication (copying data to multiple places), replication without a consensus mechanism can still end up with conflicting versions of the truth.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does requiring a majority for both reads and writes guarantee a read always sees the latest write?**

> **Model Answer:** Any two majorities out of N nodes are mathematically guaranteed to share at least one common node, because two disjoint majorities would together need more than N nodes to exist. That shared node participated in the latest successful write, so it's guaranteed to be included in any subsequent read quorum, meaning the read is guaranteed to see the latest value somewhere among the nodes it queries.

**Q: What problem does leader election actually solve in a consensus protocol like Raft?**

> **Model Answer:** Without a leader, every node would need to negotiate the order of every operation with every other node, which is slow and complex. Electing one leader for a period of time lets that leader unilaterally decide the order of operations and replicate them to followers, dramatically simplifying agreement, while the protocol still safely detects a failed leader and elects a new one with a higher term to take over.

**Q: Why is it wrong to say Paxos or Raft guarantees a system will never be unavailable?**

> **Model Answer:** These protocols guarantee safety, the group will never agree on two conflicting values, not liveness in every situation. If a leader fails, there is a real window where no writes can be accepted until a new leader is elected, and in some network partition scenarios a minority side of the cluster can't make progress at all, by design, since it can't reach quorum.

# Search Indexing & Inverted Indexes

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A search engine answers 'which documents contain this word' in milliseconds by flipping the obvious data structure inside out ahead of time, from document-to-words into **word-to-documents**.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### From raw document to a searchable inverted index

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Raw document ('The quick fox runs fast')"]:::step
    step_2["2. Tokenize (split into words, lowercase)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Remove stop words (drop 'the')"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Stem ('runs' becomes 'run')"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Update postings lists (term -> list of doc IDs)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Query time: intersecting postings lists

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Search Query"]:::client
    gateway["Search API"]:::server
    idx["Inverted Index (shard 1)"]:::server
    idx2["Inverted Index (shard 2)"]:::server
    client -->|"'quick fox'"| gateway
    gateway -->|"lookup postings for 'quick', 'fox'"| idx
    gateway -->|"lookup postings for 'quick', 'fox'"| idx2
```

#### Inverse document frequency drops as a term gets more common

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Assuming search relevance is just about whether a term is present, and ignoring that frequency and rarity across the corpus (TF-IDF or similar) are what actually separate a strong match from a coincidental one.
- ⚠️ Expecting newly written data to be instantly searchable, when most search systems batch and periodically refresh the index rather than updating it synchronously on every write.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that stop word removal and stemming are lossy, sometimes deliberately dropping or merging distinctions that matter for a specific use case, like exact legal or code search where 'running' and 'run' should not be treated as the same term.
- ⚠️ Treating a search index as a replacement for the primary database, when it's typically a derived, denormalized view built for read performance, not the durable source of truth for the data.
- ⚠️ Underestimating storage cost, a full inverted index with positions for phrase search can be comparable in size to, or larger than, the original text it was built from.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is a full inverted index dramatically faster to search than scanning every document's raw text at query time?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the expensive work, reading and tokenizing every document, happens once at index time, not on every query. At query time, the search only has to look up the already-built postings list for each search term and intersect a small number of sorted lists, work proportional to the number of matching documents, not the size of the entire corpus.

**Q: How does an inverted index support phrase search, like matching the exact phrase 'quick fox' and not just documents containing both words separately?**

> **Model Answer:** The postings list for each term stores not just which documents contain it but the specific positions within each document. A phrase query checks that the position of 'fox' in a candidate document is exactly one more than the position of 'quick', confirming adjacency, not just co-occurrence anywhere in the document.

**Q: Why do most search systems refresh their index periodically instead of making every write instantly searchable?**

> **Model Answer:** Updating an inverted index for one new or changed document can mean touching the postings list of every distinct term in that document, which is expensive to do synchronously on every single write. Batching updates and refreshing the searchable index on an interval trades a small amount of write-to-search latency for much better indexing throughput.

# Object / Blob Storage Systems

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> **Object storage** gives up the filesystem's folder-and-edit model entirely in exchange for something that scales to trillions of files across thousands of machines: every object is a whole, immutable blob addressed by a flat key, never a path you partially edit.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Uploading and replicating an object

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client (upload)"]:::client
    gateway["Object Storage API"]:::server
    s1["Storage node (rack A)"]:::server
    s2["Storage node (rack B)"]:::server
    s3["Storage node (rack C)"]:::server
    client -->|"PUT object"| gateway
    gateway -->|"replica 1"| s1
    gateway -->|"replica 2"| s2
    gateway -.->|"replica 3"| s3
```

#### Filesystem vs object storage

| Traditional filesystem | Object storage |
| :--- | :--- |
| Nested folder hierarchy, in-place partial edits | Flat key space inside buckets, objects are whole and immutable |
| Optimized for one machine's local or attached disk | Built to scale across thousands of machines and data centers |
| Fine-grained, low-latency small reads and writes | Replace-the-whole-object updates, durability via replication or erasure coding |

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Trying to use object storage like a shared network filesystem==, expecting fast partial edits or fine-grained locking that its whole-object, immutable model was never designed to provide.
- ⚠️ Assuming the folder-like structure implied by slashes in an object's key is a real, efficiently-navigable directory tree, when it's typically just a flat namespace with string prefix matching for listing.
- ⚠️ Storing huge numbers of very small, frequently-updated objects in object storage when a database or filesystem would fit that access pattern far better, and paying per-request costs that add up fast at that shape.
- ⚠️ Choosing an archive or cold tier for data that turns out to need frequent access, then absorbing large, repeated retrieval costs and multi-hour latency that a warmer tier would have avoided.
- ⚠️ ==Forgetting that object storage durability is about surviving hardware failure, not about protecting against a bad application deleting or overwriting the wrong object==, versioning or backups are still needed for that.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't you efficiently edit a single byte in the middle of an object stored in something like S3, and why is that actually a feature, not a limitation?**

> **Model Answer:** Object storage treats every object as a whole, immutable unit, updates mean uploading an entirely new version rather than modifying bytes in place. This removes the need to coordinate concurrent partial writes to the same object across a massively distributed system, which is exactly the kind of coordination problem that makes traditional shared filesystems hard to scale to the size object storage systems operate at.

**Q: What's the practical trade-off between full replication and erasure coding for object durability?**

> **Model Answer:** Full replication stores multiple complete copies of an object, simple and fast to read or reconstruct from, but uses several times the object's actual size in raw storage. Erasure coding splits the object into data and parity fragments and can tolerate losing some fragments while using meaningfully less total storage than full replication, at the cost of extra CPU work to reconstruct the object when fragments are missing.

**Q: Why is object storage considered the backbone of media-heavy systems specifically, rather than a general-purpose replacement for a database?**

> **Model Answer:** Media files like photos and video are large, written once (or replaced wholesale on edit), and read very often, exactly the access pattern object storage is optimized for: whole-object writes, massively parallel whole-object reads, and cheap-per-gigabyte durable storage. A database is optimized for small, frequent, partial updates and complex queries, a completely different shape of workload that object storage deliberately doesn't try to serve.

# Notification Delivery Systems

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Sending one notification is trivial, sending the same event to millions of devices reliably, and quietly retrying the ones that fail, is a **fan-out** and queueing problem wearing a friendly UI.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Fan-out from one event to millions of push notifications

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    trigger["Triggering Service"]:::server
    queue>"Notification Queue"]:::queue
    worker["Delivery Workers"]:::server
    dlq>"Dead Letter Queue"]:::queue
    apns["Push Provider (APNs/FCM)"]:::server
    trigger -->|"one event"| queue
    queue -->|"fan out per device"| worker
    worker -->|"deliver"| apns
    worker -.->|"repeated failure"| dlq
```

#### Retry with exponential backoff and jitter

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Attempt 1 fails (wait ~1s + jitter)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Attempt 2 fails (wait ~2s + jitter)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Attempt 3 fails (wait ~4s + jitter)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Attempt 4 fails (max retries reached)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Send to dead letter queue (stop retrying, alert or inspect)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Retry delay growth: exponential backoff vs backoff with jitter

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Sending notifications synchronously inside the request that triggered them==, which makes the triggering action's latency scale with the number of recipients instead of staying constant.
- ⚠️ ==Retrying failed deliveries immediately and aggressively without backoff==, which can turn a brief provider hiccup into a self-inflicted traffic spike that makes the outage worse.
- ⚠️ Retrying every failed delivery forever with no dead letter queue, quietly burning worker capacity on tokens or endpoints that will never succeed again.
- ⚠️ Treating push delivery as guaranteed and instant, when devices can be offline, apps uninstalled, or tokens stale, delivery is inherently best-effort even when the system itself is working correctly.
- ⚠️ Building a webhook or push system without idempotency on the receiving side, then getting duplicate notifications or duplicate side effects the moment an at-least-once retry succeeds after the original attempt actually landed.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does a notification system need a queue between the triggering event and actual delivery, instead of just delivering directly?**

> **Model Answer:** One event, like a viral post, can require delivering to millions of devices, and doing that synchronously would make the triggering request's latency scale with the number of recipients, an unbounded and unacceptable cost. A queue absorbs the fan-out asynchronously, letting the triggering request return immediately while a pool of workers handles the actual per-device delivery at its own pace.

**Q: A downstream push provider starts failing intermittently. Why is retrying immediately and repeatedly a bad idea, and what should happen instead?**

> **Model Answer:** Immediate, repeated retries add exactly the same load pattern back onto a provider that's already struggling, which can turn a brief hiccup into a sustained outage. Exponential backoff with jitter spaces retries out with increasing, randomized delays, giving the provider room to recover and avoiding a synchronized wave of retries all landing at once.

**Q: What's the difference between at-most-once and at-least-once delivery for notifications, and why do most systems pick at-least-once?**

> **Model Answer:** At-most-once fires a delivery attempt once and doesn't retry, so a transient failure means the notification is simply lost. **At-least-once** retries until success or a dead letter queue, guaranteeing delivery eventually happens if the target is reachable, at the cost of ==possible duplicates==, which is why most systems choose at-least-once and rely on idempotency on the receiving side rather than accept silent message loss.

    step_2["2. Attempt 2 fails (wait ~2s + jitter)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Attempt 3 fails (wait ~4s + jitter)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Attempt 4 fails (max retries reached)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Send to dead letter queue (stop retrying, alert or inspect)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Retry delay growth: exponential backoff vs backoff with jitter

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Sending notifications synchronously inside the request that triggered them==, which makes the triggering action's latency scale with the number of recipients instead of staying constant.
- ⚠️ ==Retrying failed deliveries immediately and aggressively without backoff==, which can turn a brief provider hiccup into a self-inflicted traffic spike that makes the outage worse.
- ⚠️ Retrying every failed delivery forever with no dead letter queue, quietly burning worker capacity on tokens or endpoints that will never succeed again.
- ⚠️ Treating push delivery as guaranteed and instant, when devices can be offline, apps uninstalled, or tokens stale, delivery is inherently best-effort even when the system itself is working correctly.
- ⚠️ Building a webhook or push system without idempotency on the receiving side, then getting duplicate notifications or duplicate side effects the moment an at-least-once retry succeeds after the original attempt actually landed.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does a notification system need a queue between the triggering event and actual delivery, instead of just delivering directly?**

> **Model Answer:** One event, like a viral post, can require delivering to millions of devices, and doing that synchronously would make the triggering request's latency scale with the number of recipients, an unbounded and unacceptable cost. A queue absorbs the fan-out asynchronously, letting the triggering request return immediately while a pool of workers handles the actual per-device delivery at its own pace.

**Q: A downstream push provider starts failing intermittently. Why is retrying immediately and repeatedly a bad idea, and what should happen instead?**

> **Model Answer:** Immediate, repeated retries add exactly the same load pattern back onto a provider that's already struggling, which can turn a brief hiccup into a sustained outage. Exponential backoff with jitter spaces retries out with increasing, randomized delays, giving the provider room to recover and avoiding a synchronized wave of retries all landing at once.

**Q: What's the difference between at-most-once and at-least-once delivery for notifications, and why do most systems pick at-least-once?**

> **Model Answer:** At-most-once fires a delivery attempt once and doesn't retry, so a transient failure means the notification is simply lost. **At-least-once** retries until success or a dead letter queue, guaranteeing delivery eventually happens if the target is reachable, at the cost of ==possible duplicates==, which is why most systems choose at-least-once and rely on idempotency on the receiving side rather than accept silent message loss.
